title: D&I4DBT Class 1 - The Digital Economy
subtitle: Multiple-choice quiz based on slides 30-72: today's digital economy, technology adoption, fundamental laws, general purpose technologies, and the consequences of digitalization.

questions.question: Which set of attributes best characterizes today's digital economy as presented in the course?
options: Confined permanently to high-tech industries and largely immaterial with no infrastructure
Highly interconnected and interdependent, with strong dependency on a few dominant players
Driven mainly by natural resources and physical assets rather than data
Loosely connected, independent actors with stable, slow-moving technology
questions.explanation: The course describes the digital economy as highly interconnected and interdependent with strong dependency on a few dominant players, changing rapidly. The 'loosely connected' option inverts these traits; the 'high-tech/immaterial' option is wrong because digitalization is spreading beyond high-tech and is 'highly virtual but not so immaterial'; the 'natural resources' option describes the old economy.

questions.question: The slides describe information and data in the digital economy using which metaphor?
questions.explanation: Data and information are framed as the new 'oil' or 'currency'. The other metaphors are not the ones used and would shift the meaning away from data as a tradable, value-bearing resource.

questions.question: How has the digital economy evolved structurally, according to the course?
options: From self-contained local machines into a hyperconnected system of interrelated heterogeneous entities governed by different, possibly conflicting logics
From immaterial data flows into purely physical infrastructure
From a hyperconnected system into a few self-contained mainframes
From a global network back into isolated local machines
questions.explanation: The slides trace evolution from self-contained, local machines (interconnected or not) into a hyperconnected system of interrelated heterogeneous entities governed by different and possibly conflicting logics. The other options reverse or distort that trajectory.

questions.question: In the old economy versus new economy comparison, which pairing is correct?
options: Old economy: diminishing returns, asset heavy; New economy: increasing returns, asset light
Old economy: increasing returns, global; New economy: diminishing returns, local
Old economy: digital world, asset light; New economy: physical world, asset heavy
Old economy: data and knowledge; New economy: natural resources
questions.explanation: The old economy is tangible, local, asset heavy, with diminishing returns; the new economy is virtual, global, asset light, with increasing returns. The other options swap the attributes between the two economies.

questions.question: According to the old-versus-new economy slide, the time to reach a 1-billion valuation changed in which way?
options: From about 20 years in the old economy to about 5 years in the new economy
It remained roughly 20 years in both
It increased because digital firms need heavier assets
From about 5 years in the old economy to about 20 years in the new economy
questions.explanation: The slide contrasts roughly 20 years to reach a billion-dollar valuation in the old economy with about 5 years in the new economy, reflecting asset-light, increasing-returns dynamics. The other options reverse or flatten this difference.

questions.question: What does the course mean by stating it is 'no longer about new versus old economies'?
options: Digitalization is blurring traditional sector borders and absorbing the divide between non-digital and digital economies
Only high-tech industries remain economically relevant
The new economy has been abandoned in favor of physical assets
questions.explanation: Digitalization rapidly blurs traditional sector borders, and the divide between the old non-digital and new digital economies is slowly being absorbed. The other options overstate disappearance or misread the convergence as a reversal.

questions.question: The course links today's digital economy to which broader characterization of industrial change?
options: The post-industrial service revolution of the 1970s only
The Digital Revolution or Fourth Industrial Revolution
questions.explanation: The digital economy is framed as the Digital Revolution or Fourth Industrial Revolution. The other options name unrelated or earlier transformations that do not match the slide's framing.

questions.question: Which statement about the materiality of the digital economy matches the course's nuance?
options: It is highly virtual but not so immaterial
Its materiality is irrelevant to its economics
It is entirely immaterial, requiring no physical infrastructure
It is purely physical with no virtual component
questions.explanation: The slides stress that the digital economy is 'highly virtual but not so immaterial', acknowledging the physical substrate (devices, networks, data centers). Treating it as fully immaterial or fully physical both miss this nuance.

questions.question: The course lists which two categories of forces shaping the digital economy?
options: Consumer fashion cycles and advertising spend
Technology adoption by businesses/individuals, and fundamental underlying laws and principles with their consequences
questions.explanation: The two shaping forces are technology adoption (by businesses and individuals) and the fundamental underlying laws and principles together with their consequences. The other options name factors not used as the organizing frame.

questions.question: Among the 'fundamental laws and principles' consequences, which list matches the course?
options: Brand loyalty, advertising, packaging, and distribution
Patent law, copyright, trademarks, and trade secrets
Convergence of networks/interconnectedness, rise and present-day divergence of the internet, affordability of technologies, and long innovation cycles
Tax policy, labor mobility, urbanization, and inflation
questions.explanation: The consequences listed are convergence of networks and interconnectedness, the rise of the internet and its present-day divergence, affordability of technologies, and long innovation cycles. The other options list unrelated economic or legal factors.

questions.question: What phenomenon does the technology S-Curve describe?
options: Immediate saturation followed by steady decline
Slow initial growth, rapid acceleration, and eventual maturity/plateau
Random fluctuation with no systematic pattern
Linear, constant growth of a technology over time
questions.explanation: The S-Curve captures slow initial adoption, rapid growth, then a plateau at maturity, forming the characteristic S shape. The linear-growth option and the other choices do not capture the non-linear, three-phase pattern.

questions.question: Christensen's S-Curve analysis distinguishes between which two dimensions of technology?
questions.explanation: Christensen's S-Curve work distinguishes component technologies from architectural technologies, each with its own S-Curve. Disruptive/sustaining is his Innovator's Dilemma framework; general-purpose vs specialized relates to Bresnahan & Trajtenberg; incremental/radical is a generic innovation distinction.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a COMPONENT technology in Christensen's S-Curve classification?
questions.explanation: Disk drives, routers, compilers, magnetic tape, and antennas are listed as component technologies. Internet browser, PC, and mobile phone are listed as architectural technologies that integrate components.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an ARCHITECTURAL technology in Christensen's S-Curve classification?
questions.explanation: Architectural technologies include computers, the PC, the mobile phone, the TV set, and the internet browser. Routers, cathode ray tubes, and magnetic tape are component technologies.

questions.question: The S-Curve material in the course is illustrated using which source?
options: Kleiner Perkins Internet Trends Report by Mary Meeker (2018)
World Economic Forum Future of Jobs Report
questions.explanation: The S-Curve adoption slides cite the Kleiner Perkins Internet Trends Report by Mary Meeker, 2018. The other reports appear elsewhere in the course but not as the S-Curve illustration source.

questions.question: The chronological 'technology adoption' progression illustrated in the course moves through which sequence of computing eras?
options: Analytical engine/Turing machine, mainframe, IBM PC compatible, mobile smartphone
questions.explanation: The adoption illustration moves from early computing (analytical engine, Turing machine) to the mainframe, then the IBM PC compatible, and on to the mobile smartphone. The other orderings scramble this historical progression.

questions.question: Why is the S-Curve said to be useful for understanding the digital economy?
options: It captures how technologies grow and mature, helping explain adoption dynamics across component and architectural levels
It shows that technology adoption is purely random
It proves that all technologies grow at the same rate
It predicts exact revenue figures for any technology
questions.explanation: The S-Curve is a descriptive lens for how technologies progress through slow growth, acceleration, and maturity at both component and architectural levels. It does not yield exact revenue predictions, uniform growth rates, or imply randomness.

questions.question: In Rogers' Technology Adoption Lifecycle, which group represents the smallest segment of adopters?
questions.explanation: Innovators are the smallest segment (~2.5%). Early Adopters are larger (~13.5%), and both the Early and Late Majority are the largest segments (~34% each).

questions.question: What is the correct order of segments in the Technology Adoption Lifecycle used in Class Assignment 1?
options: Laggards, Late majority, Early majority, Early adopters, Innovators
Innovators, Early majority, Early adopters, Laggards, Late majority
Innovators, Early adopters, Early majority, Late majority, Laggards
Early adopters, Innovators, Early majority, Late majority, Laggards
questions.explanation: The assignment lists the five segments as Innovators, Early adopters, Early majority, Late majority, Laggards, in that order. The other options misorder or reverse the sequence.

questions.question: The diffusion-of-innovations framework used in the course is attributed primarily to which set of authors?
questions.explanation: The diffusion process / technology adoption life cycle is credited to Joe M. Bohlen, George M. Beal and Everett M. Rogers. Bresnahan and Trajtenberg are associated with general purpose technologies; Brynjolfsson and McAfee with AI as a GPT.

questions.question: In Geoffrey Moore's Market Development Lifecycle, what does 'The Chasm' represent?
options: The terminal decline of an obsolete technology
The gap between early-market visionaries/enthusiasts and the pragmatic mainstream market, where firms look for niches
questions.explanation: The Chasm is the difficult gap between the early market (visionaries and technology enthusiasts) and mainstream adoption, where firms look for niches. It is neither the mainstream growth phase nor a decline or research stage.

questions.question: In Moore's refinement, which stage is characterized by 'new applications have been found and the market is experiencing growth'?
questions.explanation: The Bowling alley and Tornado stage is when new applications have been found and the market experiences growth. The Early market is the visionary/enthusiast stage, and the Chasm is the gap before mainstream adoption.

questions.question: Moore's refinement of the adoption framework was published in which Harvard Business Review article?
options: Darwin and the Demon: Innovating Within Established Enterprises
Increasing Returns and the New World of Business
questions.explanation: Moore's relevant HBR article is 'Darwin and the Demon: Innovating Within Established Enterprises' (2004). The other titles are by different authors (Iansiti & Lakhani; Westerman et al.; Brian Arthur).

questions.question: In the course's own adoption framework, which sequence of phases appears along the revenue-growth-over-time curve?
options: Decline, Maturity, the Chasm, Early stage
Early stage, the Chasm / uncertainty zone, Growth, Maturity, Decline
questions.explanation: The course framework runs Early stage, then the Chasm (uncertainty zone), then Growth, Maturity, and Decline. The other options scramble the natural progression of a technology's life cycle.

questions.question: Class Assignment 1 asks students to position which kinds of items within the adoption cycle?
options: Internet of Things, Artificial Intelligence systems, Big Data technologies, Blockchain
questions.explanation: The proposed items are Internet of Things, Artificial Intelligence systems, Big Data technologies, and Blockchain. The other lists name older technologies or office tools not used in the assignment.

questions.question: In the telephone-technology discussion, which progression of switching/transmission technologies is illustrated?
options: Analog circuits and circuit switching, then digital circuits and packet switching, then GSM, 4G, 5G
Binary logic, mainframe, PC, tactile screen
Packet switching, then circuit switching, then analog circuits
5G, then 4G, then GSM, then analog circuits
questions.explanation: The telephone curve moves from analog circuits / circuit switching to digital circuits / packet switching, then through GSM, 4G, and 5G. The 'binary logic to tactile screen' option describes the computer's progression, and the others reverse the order.

questions.question: In the computer-technology discussion, which progression of man-machine interfaces is illustrated?
options: GUI, then binary logic, then tactile screen, then mainframe
Binary logic and mainframe, then PC, then GUI, then tactile screen
Tactile screen, GUI, mainframe, binary logic
questions.explanation: The computer curve runs from binary logic and the mainframe to the PC, then the GUI, then the tactile screen. The 'packet switching / GSM / 4G / 5G' option is the telephone progression, and the other options misorder the interface evolution.

questions.question: Which job is cited as having disappeared from the telecommunications industry?
questions.explanation: Switchboard operators are the disappeared telecom job. Accounting clerks and typists are cited for the computer industry; data scientists are a current, not disappeared, role.

questions.question: Which transformation of telecom companies is correctly stated in the course?
questions.explanation: France Telecom became Orange, while British Telecom split into BT Retail, BT Wholesale, BT Openreach, and EE. The course lists Nokia, Siris, Cegetel, and LDCOM among those that did not survive ('RIP').

questions.question: Which jobs are cited as having disappeared from the computer industry?
questions.explanation: Accounting clerks and typists are the disappeared computer-industry jobs. Switchboard operators belong to the telecom example; network engineers and cloud architects are modern roles.

questions.question: Which companies are listed among the computer-industry firms that did NOT survive ('RIP')?
options: Silicon Graphics, Digital Equipment Corporation, Sun
questions.explanation: Silicon Graphics, Digital Equipment Corporation, and Sun are listed among those that did not survive. Microsoft, Oracle, and IBM are listed as transformed survivors; Orange/BT/EE are telecom firms.

questions.question: How does Utterback define a 'dominant design'?
options: The cheapest product variant in a class
The first prototype ever built in a product class
The design that wins the allegiance of the marketplace and that competitors and innovators must adhere to to gain significant following
questions.explanation: Utterback defines a dominant design as the one that wins the marketplace's allegiance, which competitors and innovators must adhere to for significant following; it is typically synthesized from prior independent innovations. Cost, chronology, and regulation are not its defining features.

questions.question: Why are dominant designs described as useful in the course?
options: They guarantee a monopoly for the firm that creates them
They help understand technology adoption and can determine the adoption lifecycle quite early in the cycle
They prevent any further innovation in a product class
They eliminate the need for the S-Curve
questions.explanation: Dominant designs are useful for understanding technology adoption and tend to determine the adoption lifecycle early in the cycle. They neither guarantee monopolies, freeze innovation, nor replace the S-Curve concept.

questions.question: In the dominant-design discussion of home/office audio and computing, which timeline of audio formats is shown?
options: LP record (1950), audio cassette (1970), audio CD (1980), audio streaming (2000)
Audio streaming (2000), audio CD (1980), audio cassette (1970), LP record (1950)
Audio CD (1950), LP record (1970), audio streaming (1980), audio cassette (2000)
questions.explanation: The audio sequence runs LP record (1950), audio cassette (1970), audio CD (1980), audio streaming (2000). The reversed-order option flips it, and the others mismatch dates or mix in computing devices.

questions.question: Information theory, foundational to the digital economy, was formalized by whom and in what year?
questions.explanation: Claude E. Shannon formalized information theory in his 1948 landmark article 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication'. McDonough (1963) and Ackoff (1967) added later developments; Moore (1965) is associated with Moore's Law.

questions.question: According to Adrian McDonough's information economics, information is best defined as:
options: The meeting between data and a problem, representing the value side
The total number of bits transmitted
The cost side of the information system
questions.explanation: McDonough defines information as the meeting between data and a problem, where data is the cost side and information is the value side. The other options conflate information with cost, raw signals, or sheer volume.

questions.question: Russell Ackoff (1967) argued that beyond a certain amount of data:
options: The amount of information actually diminishes
The amount of information continues to grow without limit
questions.explanation: Ackoff stated that beyond a certain amount of data, the amount of information diminishes, anticipating information overload. The other options contradict this diminishing-returns insight.

questions.question: Which is a key implication of Shannon's information theory highlighted in the course?
options: Signals can never be reconstructed once altered
Information is unrelated to the capacity of the media carrying it
A signal can be reconstructed at the receiving end even with partial alteration due to noise
Data and information are identical concepts
questions.explanation: Shannon's theory makes it possible to reconstruct a signal at the receiver even when noise partially alters it, and it links the amount of information to media capacity. The other options contradict these implications.

questions.question: Shannon's theory established a relationship that turned signals into what?
questions.explanation: A central implication is the relationship between information and data: signals become bits of information. The other options miss the signals-to-bits transformation at the heart of the theory.

questions.question: Who is credited with Moore's Law, and with what organization is he associated?
options: Gordon E. Moore, a founder of Intel
questions.explanation: Gordon E. Moore, one of the founders of Intel, formulated Moore's Law. Claude Shannon is tied to information theory, Geoffrey Moore to the adoption chasm, and Robert Metcalfe to Metcalfe's Law.

questions.question: How did Gordon Moore's statement of his law change between 1965 and 1975?
options: It remained doubling every 18 months throughout
From doubling every year to doubling every 2 years
From doubling every 2 years to doubling every year
From doubling every 5 years to doubling every year
questions.explanation: In 1965 Moore stated transistors in a chip double every year; in 1975 he revised it to doubling every two years for a microprocessor. The '2 years to every year' option reverses the change, and the others cite figures not given in the slides.

questions.question: Which is listed as an implication of Moore's Law?
options: Networks lose value as users increase
Miniaturisation and the disappearance of the analogue/digital frontier, leading to cyber-physical systems
questions.explanation: Moore's Law implies faster, more powerful computers, miniaturisation, and the gradual disappearance of the analogue/digital frontier (sensors-processors), enabling cyber-physical systems. The other options describe unrelated or contrary effects.

questions.question: Moore's Law is said to have blurred the frontier between which two worlds, via sensors and processors?
questions.explanation: Through sensors and processors, the analogue and digital worlds' frontier gradually disappeared, giving rise to cyber-physical systems. The other pairings are not the distinction the slide draws.

questions.question: What does Metcalfe's Law state?
options: The value of a network depends only on its subgroups
The value of a network is proportional to the number of its users
The value of a network declines as users are added
The value of a network is proportional to the square of the number of its users
questions.explanation: Metcalfe's Law holds that a network's value is proportional to the square of the number of users. The 'proportional to the number of users' option understates the effect (linear), the 'declines as users are added' option inverts it, and the 'depends only on subgroups' option describes Reed's Law.

questions.question: What does Reed's Law emphasize?
options: The importance of subgroups in network formation
The square of the number of users
The doubling of transistors over time
questions.explanation: Reed's Law emphasizes the importance of subgroups in network formation, going beyond Metcalfe's pairwise-connection view. The square-of-users is Metcalfe, transistor doubling is Moore, and signal reconstruction is Shannon.

questions.question: According to the course, the implications of Metcalfe's and Reed's Laws stress that a network is not only infrastructure but also:
options: A purely physical asset with no market role
questions.explanation: The course argues a network is infrastructure but, even more importantly, a market/industry arrangement. The other options ignore the economic-organizational role network effects play.

questions.question: Network effects, per the course, help explain how which two things occur?
options: How patents and copyrights are enforced
How economic value is generated in information-driven industries and how technology adoption is influenced by social dynamics
How interest rates and inflation interact
How transistors shrink and how signals are encoded
questions.explanation: Network effects illuminate how economic value is generated in information-driven industries and how social dynamics influence technology adoption. The other options concern unrelated technical or economic-legal mechanisms.

questions.question: Which set of laws/principles is the course grouping under 'fundamental laws and their consequences'?
options: Newton's laws, Ohm's law, Kepler's laws
Say's law, Gresham's law, Pareto principle
Shannon's information theory, Moore's Law, Metcalfe's Law, Reed's Law
Coase theorem, Arrow's theorem, Nash equilibrium
questions.explanation: The fundamental laws covered are Shannon's information theory, Moore's Law, Metcalfe's Law, and Reed's Law. The other options list physics or economics principles not used in this part of the course.

questions.question: The first consequence of the fundamental laws presented in the course is:
questions.explanation: The first consequence listed is the affordability of technologies, sourced to a WEF 2016 report. The other options misstate or contradict the course's enumerated consequences.

questions.question: The 'affordability of technologies' consequence is sourced to which organization's report?
options: World Economic Forum (Digital Transformation of Industries, 2016)
questions.explanation: Affordability is sourced to the World Economic Forum's 'Digital Transformation of Industries' (Geneva, January 2016). The ITU is cited for internet usage, and McKinsey/OECD appear elsewhere.

questions.question: The second consequence of the fundamental laws concerns:
questions.explanation: The second consequence is the convergence of information networks. Divergence is later framed as a present-day phenomenon for the internet specifically, not the general second consequence.

questions.question: Internet usage statistics in the course are sourced to which body?
questions.explanation: The rise-of-the-internet statistics cite the ITU (itu.int). The WEF is cited for affordability, OECD for digital-transformation measurement, and Bond/Meeker for internet/AI trends.

questions.question: The course characterizes 'the internet today' as the combination of which elements?
options: People, companies, machines, software, data, and network traffic
questions.explanation: The internet today is defined as people + companies + machines + software + data + network traffic. The other options omit several constituent elements named in the slide.

questions.question: What does the course mean by saying today's internet is 'diverging'?
options: All services are merging into a single undifferentiated network
The internet is shrinking back into telecom networks
The internet is being replaced by radio and TV
After a phase of convergence, distinct domains such as social networks, content/indexing, cloud computing, and emerging IoT are branching out
questions.explanation: The course depicts a move from convergence to divergence, with distinct domains (social networks, web navigation/content indexing, cloud computing, emerging IoT/5G) branching out. The other options describe merging, shrinking, or replacement, which is the opposite.

questions.question: Which examples does the course associate with the 'cloud computing' branch of the diverging internet?
questions.explanation: Cloud computing is exemplified by AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Facebook/TikTok/LinkedIn illustrate social networks; Google/Netflix/Spotify illustrate web navigation and content indexing; 5G/IoT is the emerging branch.

questions.question: The fifth consequence, 'long innovation cycles', is grounded in whose ideas about creative destruction?
questions.explanation: Long innovation cycles draw on Joseph A. Schumpeter, who emphasized creative destruction and the central role of innovation and the entrepreneur. Solow relates to the productivity paradox, Simon to the attention bottleneck, and Tirole to the common good.

questions.question: According to the long-innovation-cycles slide, roughly how long are these technology-driven economic cycles, and which sequence of drivers is shown?
options: 10 to 20 years: railways, electricity, computers, AI
50 to 60 years: mechanization, railways, electricity & chemicals, automation, computers & internet
questions.explanation: The slide describes long cycles of roughly 50 to 60 years, driven successively by mechanization, railways, electricity and chemicals, automation, and computers and the internet toward a global digital economy. The other options give wrong durations or driver sequences.

questions.question: How does Bresnahan and Trajtenberg (1992) characterize a General Purpose Technology?
options: A technology marked by pervasiveness, inherent potential for technical improvement, and innovational complementarities
A technology that cannot be improved once invented
A technology with no effect on downstream R&D productivity
A technology used only within a single industry
questions.explanation: A GPT is characterized by pervasiveness (used as input by many downstream sectors), inherent potential for technical improvement, and innovational complementarities that raise downstream R&D productivity. The other options contradict each of these defining traits.

questions.question: Which examples of General Purpose Technologies does the course give?
questions.explanation: The GPT examples are electricity, the computer, and the internet. The other lists are household/architectural devices, component technologies, or audio formats, none of which the slide labels as GPTs.

questions.question: Using electricity as a GPT example, why do General Purpose Technologies deliver their benefits with a delay?
options: Because they are too cheap to be adopted
Because they require complementary innovations across the entire value chain, such as reorganizing work and adapting infrastructure
questions.explanation: GPTs require innovation at all levels of the value chain (reorganizing work, adapting plants and infrastructure, new distribution grids), so their economy-wide benefits arrive with a delay. The other options misattribute the delay to profitability, regulation, or pricing.

questions.question: The electricity GPT example is sourced to which author?
questions.explanation: The electricity example and the delayed-benefits argument are sourced to David (1990). Bresnahan & Trajtenberg define GPTs, Brynjolfsson & McAfee discuss AI as a GPT, and Schumpeter underpins long cycles.

questions.question: According to Brynjolfsson & McAfee (2017), what is the most important general-purpose technology of our era?
questions.explanation: Brynjolfsson & McAfee identify artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, as the most important GPT of our era. The other technologies are not the ones singled out in that quote.

questions.question: What is the significance of classifying AI as a General Purpose Technology rather than a niche tool?
options: It implies AI is pervasive, improvable, and complementary, so its full benefits depend on broad complementary innovation and may arrive with a delay
It implies AI cannot be improved further
It implies AI will have no economic impact
It implies AI is confined to one downstream sector
questions.explanation: Treating AI as a GPT means it is pervasive across sectors, has potential for ongoing improvement, and exhibits innovational complementarities, so like electricity its economy-wide benefits depend on complementary innovation and may be delayed. The other options contradict the GPT definition.

questions.question: What does the course mean when it says 'all industries are going digital'?
options: Digitalization is blurring traditional sector borders and absorbing the divide between non-digital and digital economies
Industries are becoming more isolated from one another
Digital firms are reverting to physical operations
questions.explanation: Digitalization blurs traditional sector borders and absorbs the old/new economy divide across all industries. The other options restrict digitalization to tech firms, reverse it, or claim isolation, contrary to the slide.

questions.question: According to the McKinsey Digital America (2015) framing, which sectors are best positioned to further digitize?
options: Knowledge-intensive sectors such as ICT and media
questions.explanation: The 2015 report places knowledge-intensive sectors (ICT, media) best, followed by services and then capital-intensive sectors. The other options name sectors that are not at the front of the digitization race in that framing.

questions.question: The course stresses that in the race to digitalization, industries are:
options: Not all equal, with some better positioned than others
questions.explanation: The slide explicitly states 'not all industries are equal', with some better positioned (knowledge-intensive first, then services, then capital-intensive). The other options deny this differentiation.

questions.question: After knowledge-intensive sectors, which sectors does the McKinsey framing place next in digitization readiness?
options: Capital-intensive sectors, then knowledge sectors again
questions.explanation: After knowledge-intensive sectors come services sectors, then capital-intensive sectors. The other options omit or reorder these tiers.

questions.question: What is the 'productivity paradox' described in the information society?
options: Productivity and computing power are unrelated
Productivity grows relatively slowly despite remarkable increases in computer power
Computing power declines while productivity rises
Productivity grows faster than computing power
questions.explanation: The paradox, linked to Robert Solow's 1987 quip, is that productivity grows relatively slowly even as computing power increases remarkably. The other options invert or sever this relationship.

questions.question: The productivity paradox is associated with a famous 1987 quote by which economist?
questions.explanation: The paradox traces to Robert Solow, an American economist and Nobel laureate, in a 1987 New York Times article. Simon is tied to the attention bottleneck; Schumpeter to creative destruction; Tirole to the common good.

questions.question: What is the 'bottleneck' in the information society, per Herbert Simon?
options: Human attention being overwhelmed by massive amounts of information, making attention a scarce resource
questions.explanation: Herbert Simon's bottleneck is that human attention is overwhelmed by vast information, so attention becomes scarce, giving rise to the 'attention economy'. The other options describe shortages or surpluses Simon did not identify here.

questions.question: The course links scarcity and value with which principle?
options: Abundance of something creates scarcity elsewhere, and whatever is scarce becomes valuable
Abundance of everything raises all values equally
questions.explanation: The slide argues that abundance in one area creates scarcity in another, and that scarce items carry value (rarity implies value), raising the question of efficient organization. The other options contradict the rarity-value logic.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the 'several economies' the course says the digital economy comprises?
questions.explanation: The course lists the Attention, Knowledge, Sharing/collaborative, Subscription, Platform, and Access economies. The Barter Economy is not among them, making it the correct 'NOT' answer.

questions.question: What is identified as the common element uniting the 'several economies' (attention, knowledge, sharing, subscription, platform, access)?
questions.explanation: The common element across these economies is the adoption of digital technologies. The other options are neither the unifying thread the slide names nor consistent with the digital framing.

questions.question: In the concluding remarks, which are listed as OPPORTUNITIES of digital technologies?
options: Engines of growth, and new industries and business models
questions.explanation: Opportunities include digital technologies as engines of growth and as sources of new industries and business models. Digital labor, privacy, and regulation keeping pace are listed under challenges, not opportunities.

questions.question: Which are listed as CHALLENGES in the concluding remarks?
options: Engines of growth and new business models
Digital labor, privacy and protection of personal data, and whether public policy can keep pace (regulation)
questions.explanation: Challenges include digital labor, privacy and personal-data protection, and whether public policies can keep pace with technological progress (regulation). Growth engines and new models are opportunities, not challenges.

questions.question: According to the Class 1 summary, the digital economy results, among other things, from:
options: The return to physical, asset-heavy industries
Accelerated convergence (voice, data, images, sounds) and rapid adoption of technological innovations
The decline of computing power and networks
questions.explanation: The summary attributes the digital economy to accelerated convergence (human voice, data, images, sounds) and rapid adoption of technological innovations. The other options contradict the convergence-and-adoption narrative.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the summary's view of the 'digitalization of everything'?
options: It challenges some existing industries, transforms others, and blurs the borders between traditional industrial sectors
It reverses the conversion of the world into an ocean of data
It applies only to artificial intelligence
It leaves traditional industries untouched and keeps sector borders firm
questions.explanation: The summary states that the digitalization of everything has challenged some industries, is transforming others, and blurs borders between traditional sectors, while data/information/knowledge become essential. The other options deny these effects or overstate AI's exclusivity.
